title: the words on the doorpost
hook: the words on the doorpost; touching it on the way out

segments.voice: Yesterday: minyan, the count of ten so no mourner prays alone. Your line was some things need company. Were you someone's tenth? Day nineteen.

Next time you're in a Jewish friend's home, or a Jewish-owned shop, look at the right side of the front door, about shoulder height. There's often a small narrow case, wood or metal or ceramic, fixed to the frame at a slight angle. Watch people go in and out. Some walk right past it. Some reach up, touch it with their fingertips, and then touch their fingers to their lips, without breaking stride, the way you'd pat your pocket for your keys. It takes a second. Most people outside the tradition think the little case is the point. It isn't. Today: what's inside.
screen: `THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE DOOR.` → `A SMALL CASE, SLIGHTLY TILTED.` → `FINGERTIPS, THEN LIPS.`

segments.voice: Mezuzah just means doorpost. The commandment is right after the Shema, the six words from day two. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And thou shalt write them upon the door-posts of thy house, and upon thy gates." So Jews did, literally. Inside the case is a small piece of parchment, handwritten by a trained scribe with a quill and special ink, carrying the Shema and the passages around it. The case is just a case. The words are the mezuzah. It's rolled up, and on the back is often written one of God's names, Shaddai, which many read as the initials of guardian of the doors of Israel. Now the tilt. The medieval commentator Rashi said the mezuzah should hang upright. His grandson, Rabbeinu Tam, said it should lie flat. Two great teachers, one doorpost. Ashkenazi Jews, from central and eastern Europe, settled it by hanging it at an angle, a little of both. Many Sephardi Jews hang it upright. So every tilted mezuzah is a small monument to an argument nobody lost. The parchment is checked by a scribe twice every seven years, because a faded letter makes it unfit. And it goes on nearly every doorway in the home, not just the front door, though never the bathroom. Why touch it? Maimonides warned against treating it as a lucky charm. It's a reminder. Every time you cross a threshold, going out into the world or coming home from it, you pass the words: hear, love, teach them to your children, speak of them when you walk by the way. The touch says: I'm taking these with me.
screen: `MEZUZAH — DOORPOST.` · `THE WORDS ARE THE MEZUZAH.` · `UPRIGHT OR FLAT? TILT IT.` · `A REMINDER, NOT A CHARM.` · then, large: `WRITE THEM UPON THE DOOR-POSTS.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Picture the front door of your home. The frame, the handle, the way the light falls there. Think of everything you carry out of that door each morning: worries, plans, a mood. Then choose one thing you'd like to carry out instead, a line, a value, a person you're doing it for. Picture touching the doorframe as you leave. The bell holds the time.
The mezuzah. The doorpost, and the handwritten words of the Shema rolled up and fixed there. Nineteenth word.
Your line: take the words with you. Today, every time you walk through a doorway, touch the frame and remember the one thing you chose to carry. Day nineteen.

howItsDone: Jews fix a mezuzah, a handwritten parchment of the Shema passages in a case, on the right doorpost of the home's doorways, and many touch it and kiss their fingers when passing through.

original.note: Hebrew: doorpost. the word for the frame became the word for the scroll on it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Jewish decoration on the door.
what it means: the words of the Shema, handwritten and fixed to the doorpost, touched on the way in and out.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 6:9 and 11:20; the tilt settles Rashi against Rabbeinu Tam; Maimonides (Laws of Mezuzah 5:4) rejects it as an amulet.
